opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it comes down to trust. When someone brings a health question to ChatGPT, they're often at a vulnerable moment. Maybe they just got lab results they don't understand, or they're worried about a symptom at 2 a.m., or they're caring for a parent and trying to make sense of a new diagnosis. In those moments, people need to know that the answer is aimed at helping them, and nothing else.

Advertising introduces an incentive that doesn't line up with that. Even if no one intends harm, once there's a commercial interest in which product, clinic, or treatment gets mentioned, people reasonably start to wonder whether the response is shaped by that. In health, that doubt is corrosive. If people can't trust the information, they either ignore good advice or, worse, follow advice that was quietly nudged in a direction that wasn't in their interest.

There's also the sensitivity of the data. People share very personal things about their bodies, their mental health, and their medications. Keeping that information walled off from any ad-targeting system is a basic part of respecting it. We want people to feel comfortable being completely honest, because the more context they share, the better and safer the help can be.

So for me, keeping ads out isn't a nice-to-have. It's part of the foundation. If we want AI to actually improve people's health, help them understand their care, ask better questions of their doctors, and navigate a complicated system, then it has to be unambiguously on their side. Clear boundaries like this are how you earn that trust and keep it.

r001.rationale: The response says advertising creates a commercial incentive that could make people doubt whether health answers are shaped by company interests, undermining trust in the health-focused help.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to trust, and trust is the whole product when you're talking about health.

When someone opens ChatGPT Health, they're often doing it at a vulnerable moment. They've just gotten a diagnosis they don't understand, or a lab result came back with a number in red, or they're worried about a parent. In that moment, the question they're really asking is, "Can I rely on what this thing is telling me?" The second there's any possibility that the answer is shaped by who's paying for placement, that trust is gone, and I don't think you get it back.

There's a more concrete version of that too. In most consumer products, the incentive misalignment from ads is annoying but tolerable. You see a sneaker you didn't need. In health, the misalignment can actually hurt people. If a model is even slightly nudged toward recommending a particular drug, a particular supplement, a particular clinic, that's not a UX problem, that's a safety problem. And the thing about these systems is that the nudge wouldn't need to be explicit. It could be subtle framing, which option gets mentioned first, how risks get described. Users can't audit that. So the only honest way to earn the trust is to remove the incentive entirely.

I'd also say there's a clinical analogy that matters to me. We've spent decades building norms in medicine around conflicts of interest, around disclosure, around separating the person advising you from the person selling to you. Those norms exist because we learned the hard way what happens without them. If we're going to build something that millions of people treat a bit like a first conversation with a clinician, I think we inherit those obligations. We don't get to skip them because the interface is a chat box.

And honestly, from a product perspective, I think it's the right long-term bet. The value here is in being genuinely on the user's side. If people believe that, they'll bring us the questions they're embarrassed to ask anyone else, and that's where we can actually help. Advertising would trade that away for revenue that, frankly, isn't worth it.

r001.rationale: The response says ads could make health recommendations appear shaped by who pays for placement and create harmful conflicts of interest, so removing advertising removes that incentive and protects trust in the health guidance.

astra-6.text:
I think health is an area where people need to trust that the response is focused on helping them. If you’re sharing something sensitive or trying to understand a medical concern, you shouldn’t have to wonder whether a recommendation is there because it’s useful to you or because someone paid to put it there.

Keeping advertising out removes that potential conflict. It doesn’t, by itself, make the system accurate or trustworthy—we still have to earn that through the quality of the responses, privacy protections, and being clear about limitations. But it helps make the relationship straightforward: the system is there to support you in understanding your health.

r001.rationale: The response says users should not have to wonder whether a health recommendation is useful or paid for, and that removing ads removes this potential conflict.
